_doc: THE SHELF: which machine you sit at, and what is on it.
A session is the MACHINE, not the toolchain. PRISM's worker branches on more than four hosts --
DJGPP with Allegro, DJGPP with the VGA registers, Watcom's DOS4GW, X11, MGL, Win32 -- but those
are differences between BUILDS, and nobody sitting at the machine could tell you which one they
were in. MAME and Quake are both DOS programs; Quake and Quake II are both X clients.
So this file names four machines and says what each one runs. Every entry points at a program
descriptor in web/programs/ (the GAME: what it is, what data it needs, what its keys do) and,
where the target has several platform layers, at the VARIANT that belongs to this machine. Quake
appears four times because id wrote four platform layers for it, and each one is a different
Unit counts are NOT here. The server resolves them from targets/*.json when the page asks, so a
number on the screen is one the build would produce rather than one somebody typed.

machines.name: DOS
machines._jumpbump: The FILE NAME is derived, not copied, and this says so rather than letting it pass as evidence. The tree carries no makefile and names no executable anywhere in readme.txt or source.txt, so there is nothing to read it off; JUMPBUMP is taken from the one name the source does state -- main.c does strcpy(datfile_name, "jumpbump.dat"). The date is the year on the game's own title, 1998; the source release is a year later (source.txt: 'by Brainchild Design in 99') and the tree itself reaches us through a 2002 CVS import, so no file date in it means anything.

machines.name: Linux
machines._quake2gl: quake2.gl is the same quake2 binary with ref_gl.so beside it (vid_ref gl), the renderer the 3.19 Makefile.i386 built; the file name is the shelf's, so the two renderers can sit side by side.
machines._glquake: glquake.glx is Makefile.linuxi386's own name for the GLX build. Its date is the day id released the source under the GPL, which is when that makefile target reached anyone outside id; the 1997 GLQuake binaries were Windows ones.
machines._jumpnbump: The SAME GAME as the DOS shelf's JUMPBUMP.EXE, over the other platform layer -- which is why it earns a second slot rather than replacing the first. Its build is a Linux one (the Makefile calls sdl-config and links -lSDL), so this is where it belongs. The date is the tag's own tree, the 2002 CVS import; the game is 1998 and the DOS entry says so.
machines._jumpnbump_sdl2: AND THE THIRD LAYER BESIDE IT, whose file name is the SHELF's and not the program's. Both Makefiles build a binary called `jumpnbump`, so a real Linux box could not hold the two in one directory and a listing showing both already compresses reality; saying so is cheaper than pretending otherwise. The convention is quake.svga's, three rows up. What actually separates them is recorded rather than invented: one links -lSDL and -lSDL_mixer, the other -lSDL2 and -lSDL2_mixer -- which is what ldd would show -- and each prints its own version on its credits line, measured on screen rather than read off a tag: 1.51 there, 1.80-dev here.

machines.name: SUN
machines._one: One program, and it is the whole reason the machine exists: id shipped sys_sun.c and vid_sunx.c with WinQuake and nothing had ever been compiled against them. A machine with one program on it is a thin shelf; a machine with none is a promise.

machines.name: Windows
machines._names: An icon is labelled with the program's title, and the two GL builds share theirs with the software ones, so they name themselves: GLQUAKE is id's own name for glquake.exe; QUAKE II GL is the same quake2.exe set to load ref_gl.dll.
machines._icons: The icons are the PROGRAM's own files, pointed at where they sit in its source tree -- a browser decodes .ico natively, so there is no conversion step and no build artefact to keep in step. And they are here and on no other machine because an icon is a Windows idea: a DOS or X11 program never had one, and drawing something for it would be inventing evidence.
